title: The Gravitational Wave Foreground from Galactic Cataclysmic Variables in LISA
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, submitted to Physical Review D
summary: Electromagnetic observations have been the primary medium for studying cataclysmic variable (CV) systems, capitalizing on the invaluable opportunity they present to study binary stellar evolution and accretion. The launch of the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) mission, however, will enable a multi-messenger perspective of the population. We extend previous work to explore the gravitational wave (GW) spectra sourced by a local and Galactic population of CVs. Using the Bayesian LISA Inference Package (BLIP), we simulate LISA data containing these CV populations to understand their impact and our ability to jointly model CV and double white dwarf (DWD) GW spectra. While we find that a local CV population has negligible effect on the LISA datastream, a Galactic CV population will have a signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 76, depending on the characteristics of the DWD population present, and will bias existing DWD spectral models if ignored. Current approaches struggle to accurately recover both populations' respective spectra, calling for the creation of multi-component spectral models that include GW contributions from both CVs and DWDs. These results point toward a promising future for the study of CVs with LISA.

AI.tldr: LISA will detect a Galactic cataclysmic variable GW foreground (SNR ~76) that biases double white dwarf spectral models if ignored, motivating joint multi-component spectral models.
AI.motivation: Cataclysmic variables (CVs) have been studied almost exclusively through electromagnetic observations, which offer unique insight into binary stellar evolution and accretion. LISA's launch will introduce a gravitational-wave (GW) perspective, so it is necessary to quantify how CV populations contaminate and interact with the LISA datastream—particularly alongside the dominant double white dwarf (DWD) foreground.
AI.method: The authors extend prior work by modeling GW spectra from both a local and a Galactic CV population. Using the Bayesian LISA Inference Package (BLIP), they simulate LISA data containing these CV populations and perform joint inference of CV and DWD GW spectra to assess parameter recovery and systematic bias.
AI.result: A local CV population has a negligible effect on the LISA datastream. A Galactic CV population yields a signal-to-noise ratio of roughly 76—depending on the characteristics of the DWD population—and biases existing DWD spectral models when neglected. Current approaches struggle to simultaneously and accurately recover both populations' spectra.
AI.conclusion: Multi-component spectral models incorporating GW contributions from both CVs and DWDs are required for unbiased LISA inference. These findings indicate a promising future for GW studies of CVs with LISA.

title: Euclid DR1 Legacy Science on Ultracool Dwarfs: New URLD candidates in Euclid and SPHEREx
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables, 2 appendices with 3 tables and 4 figures: submitted to A&A
summary:
Unusually red L dwarfs (URLDs) probe extreme atmospheric conditions in the substellar regime, where enhanced dust opacity, cloud structure, and surface gravity effects challenge standard brown dwarf models. As free-floating analogues of young giant exoplanets, they provide key benchmarks for interpreting low-resolution infrared spectra from current and future wide-field space missions.
  The goal is to identify new red L dwarf candidates both photometrically and spectroscopically in the first data release (DR1) of the Euclid space mission. The area covered is about 1,900 and 50 square degrees in the wide and deep survey, respectively.
  We used colour cuts in multiple colour-colour diagrams combined with point-source and quality criteria to identify candidate red L dwarfs in both the Euclid wide and deep survey fields. We cross-matched photometric candidates with the SPHEREx mission and Euclid red grism spectra to confirm spectroscopic properties and evaluate bolometric magnitudes and colours.
  We identified 1202 and 38 red L dwarf candidates in the Euclid wide and deep surveys, respectively. Spectroscopic follow-up and archival cross-matching confirm a substantial new population of red L dwarfs. Distance-independent diagnostics show that these objects occupy distinct loci characterised by enhanced condensate opacity and significant redness.
  Euclid vastly expands the census of unusually red L dwarfs. While preliminary spectral classifications suggest many of these new candidates are intermediate-age (Pleiades-like) objects, a subset exhibits extremely red signatures indicative of very young, low-gravity (<=10 Myr) atmospheres, providing vital benchmarks for young exoplanet research.

AI.tldr: Euclid DR1 yields 1202 red L dwarf candidates in the wide survey and 38 in the deep survey, confirmed photometrically and spectroscopically via SPHEREx and Euclid grism data, substantially expanding the census of unusually red L dwarfs.
AI.motivation: Unusually red L dwarfs (URLDs) trace extreme substellar atmospheres with enhanced dust opacity, cloud structure, and low surface gravity. As free-floating analogues of young giant exoplanets, they are key benchmarks for interpreting low-resolution infrared spectra from current and future wide-field space missions.
AI.method: Colour cuts across multiple colour-colour diagrams, combined with point-source and quality criteria, applied to Euclid DR1 wide (~1,900 deg²) and deep (~50 deg²) survey fields to select photometric candidates. Candidates were cross-matched with SPHEREx photometry and Euclid red grism spectra to confirm spectroscopic properties and derive bolometric magnitudes and colours.
AI.result: 1202 and 38 red L dwarf candidates identified in the wide and deep surveys, respectively. Spectroscopic follow-up and archival cross-matching confirm a substantial new population; distance-independent diagnostics place them on distinct loci indicating enhanced condensate opacity and pronounced redness.
AI.conclusion: Euclid greatly expands the census of unusually red L dwarfs. Preliminary spectral classifications suggest many candidates are intermediate-age (Pleiades-like), while a subset shows extremely red signatures consistent with very young, low-gravity (<=10 Myr) atmospheres, offering vital benchmarks for young exoplanet research.

title: Receiving Exoplanet Messages with Gravitational-wave Carriers: The Gravitational-wave Radial Velocity Method
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures. Published by The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Gravitational-wave (GW) radial velocity (RV) may offer a new method for detecting exoplanets, one that would primarily target planets orbiting GW-emitting, ultracompact, post-main-sequence stellar objects such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes. In this work we show that while similar to electromagnetic-based RV, this GW-based method depends on the ''phase modulation index'' (PMI), a parameter that is more sensitive to high-mass, long-period exoplanets. We investigate the potential of GW RV for GW sources in both the mid-frequency spectrum (where the upcoming LISA mission will operate) and the high-frequency spectrum (where the current LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) observatories operate). Remarkably, we find that the PMI increases by a factor of $\sim \mathrm{O}\left(10^4 - 10^6\right)$ going from the mid-frequency to the high-frequency GW spectrum, which results in a greater redistribution of observed power due to the exoplanet's presence. By analyzing the power content of the observed GW signal, we derive analytic expressions to predict the GW carrier frequency power loss due to the exoplanet and the signal-to-noise ratio of the GW source and the exoplanet. We also explore the effects of the additional Doppler effect caused by the motion of the GW observatory and the potential for GW source parameter bias introduced by the presence of an undetected exoplanet. All of this helps us better understand where the GW RV method may work best in the exoplanet mass-period discovery space.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes gravitational-wave radial velocity (GW RV) as a new exoplanet detection method targeting planets around ultracompact post-main-sequence GW sources, showing that the phase modulation index rises by ~10^4–10^6 from the LISA band to the LVK band, and deriving analytic expressions for carrier power loss and detection signal-to-noise.
AI.motivation: Electromagnetic RV detection cannot readily target the ultracompact, post-main-sequence objects (white dwarfs, neutron stars, black holes) that emit gravitational waves; a GW-based RV analog would open exoplanet discovery space around such sources across both mid-frequency (LISA) and high-frequency (LVK) bands.
AI.method: The authors formulate GW RV as a phase/Doppler modulation of the emitted GW signal, characterized by a phase modulation index (PMI) more sensitive to high-mass, long-period planets. They compare the mid-frequency (LISA) and high-frequency (LVK) spectra, analyze the power content of the observed GW signal to derive analytic expressions for carrier-frequency power loss and for the signal-to-noise ratio of the GW source and the exoplanet, and also examine Doppler effects from the observatory's motion and parameter bias induced by an undetected exoplanet.
AI.result: The PMI increases by a factor of ~O(10^4–10^6) from the mid-frequency to the high-frequency GW spectrum, producing a greater redistribution of observed power due to the exoplanet. Analytic expressions are obtained for the GW carrier power loss and for the source/planet SNR; additional observatory-motion Doppler effects and source-parameter bias from an undetected exoplanet are characterized.
AI.conclusion: The GW RV method is most promising in the high-frequency (LVK-type) band, where the much larger PMI makes exoplanet-induced modulation more detectable; the results map where the method performs best in the exoplanet mass-period discovery space and highlight parameter-bias implications for GW source inference.

title: Multimessenger Exoplanets: Combining Infrared Excess and Astrometry with Gravitational-wave Detections of Double White Dwarf Exoplanets
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Published by The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Multimessenger astrophysics provides a powerful framework for characterizing astrophysical systems through multiple, independent signals rather than relying solely on electromagnetic (EM) observations. While most prior multimessenger studies have focused on the properties of ultracompact objects, recent work has shown that gravitational waves (GWs) detectable with the upcoming Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) observatory can also be used to detect exoplanets orbiting stellar remnants. In particular, this includes circumbinary planets around tight double white dwarf (DWD) systems. This population is unique: no such planets are currently known around DWDs, and only a handful of circumbinary planets around main-sequence stars and planets orbiting white dwarfs (WDs) have been identified. Independent EM confirmation will be essential, especially for the first GW-detected exoplanets, to validate this method. While EM techniques are unlikely to efficiently survey large populations of DWDs, GW detection followed by targeted EM confirmation provides one pathway for identifying and characterizing these systems. Using a representative case, the known DWD ZTF J2243+5242 scaled to a fiducial distance of 150 pc, we compute the detectability of circumbinary exoplanets via LISA GW observations. We then demonstrate two complementary EM techniques--JWST infrared (IR) excess and Gaia or Habitable Worlds Observatory astrometry--that could independently confirm a GW-detected planet in this fiducial system. We present the first exploration of IR excess around DWDs as a viable exoplanet detection method, extending its established use for solitary WDs. Both EM techniques overlap with regions of parameter space where LISA is sensitive to DWD exoplanets, enabling robust confirmation and characterization.

AI.tldr: The paper explores how LISA gravitational-wave observations can detect circumbinary exoplanets around tight double white dwarfs, and demonstrates that JWST infrared excess and Gaia/Habitable Worlds Observatory astrometry can independently confirm such GW-detected planets, using ZTF J2243+5242 scaled to 150 pc as a fiducial case.
AI.motivation: Multimessenger astrophysics has mainly targeted ultracompact objects, but LISA GWs can also reveal exoplanets orbiting stellar remnants, including circumbinary planets around double white dwarfs. No such planets are currently known, and independent electromagnetic confirmation is essential to validate the GW detection method for the first GW-detected exoplanets.
AI.method: Using the known DWD ZTF J2243+5242 scaled to a fiducial distance of 150 pc, the authors compute the detectability of circumbinary exoplanets via LISA GW observations, then demonstrate two complementary EM techniques—JWST infrared excess (first exploration of IR excess around DWDs) and Gaia/Habitable Worlds Observatory astrometry—for independent confirmation.
AI.result: Both EM techniques overlap with regions of parameter space where LISA is sensitive to DWD exoplanets, enabling robust confirmation and characterization. The IR excess method, previously established for solitary WDs, is extended to DWDs for the first time.
AI.conclusion: GW detection followed by targeted EM confirmation provides a viable pathway for identifying and characterizing circumbinary exoplanets around DWDs, since EM surveys alone are unlikely to efficiently cover large DWD populations.

title: The Eclipsing $δ$ Scuti Binary HIP 7666: Absolute Dimensions and Pulsation Properties
comment: 22 pages, including 8 figures and 5 tables, accepted for publication in AJ
summary: We present a comprehensive analysis of the pulsating eclipsing binary HIP 7666 (TIC 308953703), containing a $δ$ Sct-type component, based on 120-s TESS photometry and 63 newly acquired high-resolution echelle spectra. While previous orbital solutions were limited by sparse spectroscopic sampling, our extensive radial velocity (RV) measurements enable a robust determination of the system's physical parameters. The primary has an effective temperature of $T_{\rm eff,A}$ = 7376$\pm$72 K and a projected rotational velocity of $v_{\rm A}\sin i$ = 56.6$\pm$5.3 km s$^{-1}$. Joint modeling of the light and RV curves shows that HIP 7666 is a detached system in a circular orbit, with Roche-lobe filling factors of $f_{\rm A}$ = 57 \% and $f_{\rm B}$ = 44 \%. The masses and radii are determined to better than 2 \% precision: $M_{\rm A}$ = 1.822$\pm$0.029 $M_\odot$, $R_{\rm A}$ = 2.154$\pm$0.017 $R_\odot$ for the primary, and $M_{\rm B}$ = 1.246$\pm$0.020 $M_\odot$, $R_{\rm B}$ = 1.170$\pm$0.015 $R_\odot$ for the secondary. The binary-based distance (316$\pm$8 pc) agrees well with the Gaia DR3 parallax-based distance (313$\pm$1 pc), validating the derived system parameters. Frequency analysis of the light-curve residuals reveals 15 significant signals, predominantly in the $δ$ Sct pulsation frequency range. PARSEC evolutionary tracks indicate an age of $\sim$0.9 Gyr and a supersolar metallicity ($Z=0.03$), with the primary on the main sequence and the secondary located close to the zero-age main sequence. Galactic kinematics place HIP 7666 in the thin disk.

AI.tldr: Comprehensive characterization of the pulsating eclipsing binary HIP 7666 (TIC 308953703) using TESS photometry and 63 new echelle spectra, yielding precise (<2%) dynamical masses and radii, a binary distance consistent with Gaia, 15 δ Sct pulsation frequencies, and an age/metallicity of ~0.9 Gyr and Z=0.03.
AI.motivation: Previous orbital solutions for this δ Sct-containing detached binary were limited by sparse spectroscopic sampling; denser radial-velocity coverage is needed to robustly determine physical parameters and enable asteroseismic and evolutionary interpretation.
AI.method: Analysis of 120-s cadence TESS photometry combined with 63 newly acquired high-resolution echelle spectra. Radial velocities from spectroscopy plus light-curve modeling (joint fit of light and RV curves) to derive orbital and physical parameters; frequency analysis of light-curve residuals for pulsations; comparison with PARSEC evolutionary tracks and Galactic kinematics.
AI.result: Primary: Teff,A = 7376±72 K, vA sin i = 56.6±5.3 km/s. Detached, circular orbit with Roche-lobe filling factors f_A = 57%, f_B = 44%. Masses/radii to <2%: M_A = 1.822±0.029 Msun, R_A = 2.154±0.017 Rsun; M_B = 1.246±0.020 Msun, R_B = 1.170±0.015 Rsun. Binary distance 316±8 pc agrees with Gaia DR3 (313±1 pc). Fifteen significant pulsation signals in the δ Sct range. PARSEC tracks give age ~0.9 Gyr, Z=0.03; primary on main sequence, secondary near ZAMS; kinematics place system in the thin disk.
AI.conclusion: HIP 7666 is a well-characterized detached eclipsing binary with a δ Sct primary, providing precise (sub-2%) benchmark masses and radii, a Gaia-consistent distance, an asteroseismically rich pulsation spectrum, and consistent evolutionary/thin-disk kinematic classification—establishing it as a useful benchmark for stellar modeling.

title: Calibrated Period-Luminosity Relations for Mira variables in the Large Magellanic Cloud in the Vera C. Rubin Observatory $zy$-band Photometric Systems
comment: AJ accepted, 11 pages, 6 figures and 1 table
summary: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space Time (LSST) is expected to discover numerous Mira variables in nearby galaxies, enabling their application for the cosmic distance scale. Miras are excellent distance indicators at infrared wavelengths, and therefore their period-luminosity (PL) relations in reddest $zy$ photometric systems will be crucial in the LSST era. We present first empirical $zy$-band PL relation for 85 oxygen-rich (O-rich) Miras located in the Large Magellanic Cloud based on time-series observations collected using the Dark Energy Camera (DECam) at the Víctor M. Blanco 4-m Telescope. The DECam photometry was directly calibrated using the Rubin Observatory Data Preview 2 (DP2) data. The observed PL relations were found to exhibit a break around a period of $\sim 300$ days, and therefore we only derived and calibrated the PL relations for Miras with a period shorter than $300$ days. We also explored the Rubin LSST DP2 data for known Mira variables in three Local Group dwarf galaxies. The $zy$-band light curves of Miras in IC 1613 are too sparsely sampled, whereas the DP2 observations of NGC 6822 and the Sagittarius Dwarf Irregular Galaxy cover only a short temporal baseline. For an O-rich Mira in NGC 6822, we obtain a distance modulus $μ= 23.32\pm0.24$~mag in good agreement with the literature. Significantly improved temporal coverage is expected in the first official Rubin LSST data release that will enable a robust validation of the PL relation in these nearby systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first empirical period-luminosity (PL) relations in the zy bands for 85 O-rich Miras in the Large Magellanic Cloud, calibrated with DECam photometry tied to Rubin Observatory Data Preview 2, and explores DP2 data for Miras in three Local Group dwarf galaxies.
AI.motivation: LSST is expected to discover many Miras in nearby galaxies, making them valuable for the cosmic distance scale. Miras are strong infrared distance indicators, so their PL relations in the reddest zy photometric systems will be essential in the LSST era.
AI.method: Time-series DECam observations (Víctor M. Blanco 4-m Telescope) of 85 O-rich Miras in the LMC, with photometry directly calibrated against Rubin Observatory DP2 data. PL relations were derived and calibrated only for periods shorter than 300 days due to an observed break around ~300 days. DP2 data were also inspected for known Miras in IC 1613, NGC 6822, and the Sagittarius Dwarf Irregular Galaxy.
AI.result: The zy-band PL relations exhibit a break near ~300 days. DP2 light curves are too sparsely sampled for IC 1613 and cover only short baselines for NGC 6822 and Sagittarius Dwarf Irregular Galaxy. For one O-rich Mira in NGC 6822, a distance modulus of μ = 23.32 ± 0.24 mag was obtained, consistent with literature values.
AI.conclusion: First empirical zy-band PL relations for O-rich Miras are established, providing a foundation for Mira-based distances in the LSST era. Robust validation in nearby systems awaits the improved temporal coverage of the first official Rubin LSST data release.

title: SN Progenitors of SNRs in OB Associations in the LMC. I. Assessment of Methodology Using N63A
summary: Color--magnitude diagrams (CMDs) can constrain the progenitor masses of supernova remnants (SNRs), but mass estimates for massive stars are affected by limited temperature sensitivity, extinction, crowding, and nebular contamination. We use the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) SNR N63A and its OB association LH83 as a benchmark to evaluate CMD-based mass estimates. Among the tested diagnostics, the extinction-corrected MCPS $B$ vs. $U-B$ CMD provides the most useful constraint on the massive-star population. The $V$ vs. $B-V$ CMD is less reliable, while the reddening-free $W$-$Q$ diagram does not improve individual mass estimates because of its larger photometric uncertainties. Gaia EDR3 recovers bright stars missing or saturated in MCPS but provides weaker separation among the hottest stars. For seven spectroscopically classified stars, the $B$ vs. $U-B$ CMD-based masses are lower than the HR-diagram masses inferred using the same MIST tracks by $8.0~M_\odot$ on average, with a scatter of $7.0~M_\odot$. Isochrone comparisons suggest that most of the massive stars in LH83 formed about 7-15 Myr ago, complicating progenitor mass estimates based on the present-day mass function. Nevertheless, the masses of D243-1a and D243-2, stellar lifetimes predicted by the MIST models, and the empirical bubble-size-progenitor-mass relation suggest a progenitor mass of order 25-30 $M_\odot$. Our results highlight the potential and limitations of this approach for studying other LMC SNRs in OB associations.

AI.tldr: Using LMC SNR N63A and its OB association LH83 as a benchmark, the authors evaluate CMD-based progenitor mass estimates for massive stars, finding the extinction-corrected MCPS B vs. U−B CMD most useful while V vs. B−V and W−Q diagrams are less reliable, and inferring a progenitor mass of order 25–30 M☉.
AI.motivation: CMD-based progenitor mass estimates for SNRs are affected by limited temperature sensitivity, extinction, crowding, and nebular contamination. The authors use N63A/LH83 as a benchmark to assess which photometric diagnostics are actually reliable.
AI.method: They compare several CMD/diagram diagnostics (extinction-corrected MCPS B vs. U−B, V vs. B−V, reddening-free W−Q, and Gaia EDR3 photometry) against the massive-star population of LH83. For seven spectroscopically classified stars, CMD-based masses are compared with HR-diagram masses from the same MIST tracks, and isochrone fitting constrains the star formation epoch.
AI.result: The extinction-corrected MCPS B vs. U−B CMD gives the most useful constraint; V vs. B−V is less reliable and W−Q does not improve individual masses due to larger photometric uncertainties. Gaia EDR3 recovers bright/saturated stars but separates the hottest stars less well. CMD-based masses are lower than HR-diagram masses by 8.0 M☉ on average (scatter 7.0 M☉). Isochrones suggest most massive stars formed ~7–15 Myr ago.
AI.conclusion: Despite complications from the present-day mass function, masses of D243-1a and D243-2, MIST stellar lifetimes, and the empirical bubble-size–progenitor-mass relation jointly indicate a progenitor mass of order 25–30 M☉. The work highlights both the potential and the limitations of CMD-based progenitor mass estimates for LMC SNRs in OB associations.

title: Squeezing Drives Southward Magnetic Field Enhancement During 10 May 2024 CME-CME Interaction
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJL. 15 pages, 7 figures
summary: The southward magnetic field carried by coronal mass ejections (CMEs) is a key driver of space weather events, yet how interacting CMEs amplify this field remains debated. The 10 May 2024 event, which produced the strongest geomagnetic storm since 2003, offers an ideal testbed for this question. Combining multi-spacecraft observations with high-resolution controlled numerical experiments, we track the CMEs continuously from their origin near the solar surface to beyond Earth, and find that inherent squeezing during CME-CME interactions generates the sustained enhancement of the southward field, exceeding 60 nT in magnitude near Earth. First driven by the dynamic pressure of the trailing CME and later maintained by magnetic and thermal pressures at the CME-CME interface, squeezing transforms the preceding CME from a bulky cloud into a flattened "pancake" structure, prevents expansion-induced field decay, and maintains an amplified southward field over long distances. The strength of this enhancement scales with the intensity of the squeezing. Our findings establish a direct link between CME-CME interaction and strong southward fields, laying a physics-based foundation for understanding and forecasting the geoeffectiveness of interacting CMEs.

AI.tldr: Inherent squeezing during CME-CME interactions amplifies and sustains the southward magnetic field, explaining the record 10 May 2024 storm.
AI.motivation: The southward magnetic field in CMEs drives space weather, but how interacting CMEs amplify this field remains debated; the record 10 May 2024 storm provides an ideal testbed.
AI.method: Combines multi-spacecraft observations with high-resolution controlled numerical experiments, tracking CMEs continuously from near the solar surface to beyond Earth.
AI.result: Squeezing during CME-CME interactions generates sustained southward field exceeding 60 nT near Earth; first driven by trailing CME dynamic pressure, later by magnetic/thermal pressure at the interface, flattening the preceding CME into a "pancake," preventing expansion-induced field decay, and scaling with squeezing intensity.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a direct link between CME-CME interaction and strong southward fields, providing a physics-based foundation for understanding and forecasting the geoeffectiveness of interacting CMEs.

title: High-resolution Observations of Physical Properties of Dynamic Fibrils Around a Sunspot
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures; accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Understanding the formation and evolution of dynamic fibrils (DFs) in active regions is essential for uncovering the physical processes operating in the highly structured and magnetized solar atmosphere. High-resolution chromospheric observations from the New Vacuum Solar Telescope (NVST) show DFs with periodic up-and-down motions. We carry out a statistical analysis of 176 DFs around a sunspot. The mean values of deceleration, maximum velocity, maximum length, and duration of the DFs are $120 \boldsymbol{\pm 43}~\mathrm{m~s^{-2}}$, $15.9 \boldsymbol{\pm 4.5}~\mathrm{km~s^{-1}}$, $1.13 \boldsymbol{\pm 0.48}~\mathrm{Mm}$, and $270 \boldsymbol{\pm 63}~\mathrm{s}$, respectively. Several pairs of parameters exhibit correlations, most notably a clear positive correlation between deceleration and maximum velocity. The consistency between the periodicities of DFs and running penumbral waves is first identified. We further find that DFs in regions with more vertical magnetic fields exhibit larger decelerations and shorter periods, whereas those in regions with more horizontal magnetic fields exhibit the opposite behavior. These results, together with the presence of running penumbral waves, support the interpretation that DFs are driven by slow magnetoacoustic waves. Furthermore, the multiwavelength signatures of DFs from the chromosphere to the corona imply a potential contribution to energy transport and heating in the solar atmosphere.

AI.tldr: A statistical study of 176 dynamic fibrils observed with NVST links their periodic motions to running penumbral waves and slow magnetoacoustic wave driving, with magnetic field inclination controlling their kinematic properties.
AI.motivation: Dynamic fibrils (DFs) are ubiquitous in active regions, and understanding their formation and evolution is key to revealing the physical processes in the highly structured, magnetized solar atmosphere. The study aims to characterize DF kinematics statistically and test competing interpretations of their driving mechanism.
AI.method: High-resolution chromospheric observations from the New Vacuum Solar Telescope (NVST) were used to identify DFs with periodic up-and-down motions around a sunspot. A statistical analysis of 176 DFs was performed, measuring deceleration, maximum velocity, maximum length, and duration, and examining parameter correlations, oscillation periodicities (compared with running penumbral waves), and dependence on local magnetic field inclination, complemented by multiwavelength signatures from chromosphere to corona.
AI.result: Mean values: deceleration 120 ± 43 m s^-2, maximum velocity 15.9 ± 4.5 km s^-1, maximum length 1.13 ± 0.48 Mm, duration 270 ± 63 s. Several parameter pairs are correlated, most notably a clear positive correlation between deceleration and maximum velocity. DF periodicities are found to be consistent with those of running penumbral waves (first identified). DFs in more vertical-field regions show larger decelerations and shorter periods, while those in more horizontal-field regions show the opposite.
AI.conclusion: The results, together with the presence of running penumbral waves, support the interpretation that DFs are driven by slow magnetoacoustic waves. Multiwavelength signatures from chromosphere to corona further suggest a potential contribution of DFs to energy transport and heating in the solar atmosphere.

title: Numerical experiments on sunspot penumbral flows
comment: 7 pages, 9 figures, 1 movie; accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We present 3D radiative magnetohydrodynamic simulations of sunspots with a self-consistently generated penumbra. We analyze the impact of resolution, surrounding opposite-polarity fields and subsurface large-scale flows on the structure and stability of the simulated penumbra. Extended penumbral filaments are obtained for a subset of the simulations. These were run at 25 km (15 km) horizontal (vertical) resolution and with initial conditions favoring fields with strong horizontal components in the penumbral region. The surface velocities in these simulations are consistent with observations of Evershed flow. The main driving mechanism remains the same as illustrated previously in Rempel (2012). The most successful simulations produce extended penumbrae using a potential magnetic field top boundary, in contrast to previous simulations of extended penumbra with an artificial enhancement of horizontal magnetic field at the top boundary.

AI.tldr: 3D radiative MHD simulations self-consistently generate extended sunspot penumbrae at 25 km horizontal / 15 km vertical resolution, with surface flows consistent with the Evershed flow and driven by the mechanism of Rempel (2012), using a potential-field top boundary.
AI.motivation: Prior extended-penumbra simulations relied on artificial enhancement of the horizontal magnetic field at the top boundary; the authors aim to reproduce penumbrae self-consistently and to assess how resolution, surrounding opposite-polarity fields, and subsurface large-scale flows affect penumbral structure and stability.
AI.method: 3D radiative magnetohydrodynamic simulations of sunspots with a self-consistently generated penumbra; a parameter study varying numerical resolution (25 km horizontal, 15 km vertical for the successful runs), surrounding opposite-polarity fields, and subsurface large-scale flows; initial conditions favoring fields with strong horizontal components in the penumbral region; a potential magnetic field top boundary.
AI.result: Extended penumbral filaments form only in a subset of runs—those at 25 km (15 km) horizontal (vertical) resolution with initial conditions favoring strong horizontal fields in the penumbral region. Surface velocities in these simulations are consistent with Evershed flow observations.
AI.conclusion: Extended penumbrae can be produced self-consistently with a potential-field top boundary, without artificial horizontal-field enhancement; the main driving mechanism is the same as in Rempel (2012), and penumbra formation is sensitive to resolution, initial field geometry, ambient opposite-polarity flux, and subsurface flows.

title: Asteroseismology of blue straggler stars in $ω$ Centauri. Stellar collisions as a possible formation scenario
comment: Accepted for the publication in A&A Letter, 4 pages, 5 figures plus 5 pages of the Appendix
summary:
Context. Blue stragglers are intriguing stars that appear more massive and younger than expected from single-star evolution, yet their evolutionary histories remain elusive because of the multiple possible formation channels. A promising and poorly explored avenue for addressing this problem is asteroseismology, which provides the most stringent constraints on internal structure and evolution.
  Aims. We investigate five SX Phoenicis stars from the core of the globular cluster ωCentauri that pulsate in two radial modes and occupy the blue-straggler region of the colour-magnitude diagram. Seismic models are constructed assuming a collisional origin and compared with our previous seismic studies based on single-star evolution. For comparison, we also explore a binary-evolution scenario involving mass transfer for one of the stars.
  Methods. The evolution of the parent stars is computed with MESA. The collision is then modelled with the MMAMS code, which reconstructs the merger remnant using an entropic variable. The subsequent evolution is followed with MESA up to the current age of the cluster. Finally, we construct seismic models reproducing the observed frequencies of the two radial modes.
  Results. We present the first seismic modelling of SX Phe stars (blue stragglers) based on the collision-formation scenario. Convective-core overshooting is essential for rejuvenation and for obtaining seismic models in the main-sequence phase of evolution, but it is not always sufficient. Whether a merger remnant undergoes rejuvenation depends in a complex way on the masses of the parent stars, metallicity, and collision time. We identify three evolutionary behaviours: no, delayed, and immediate rejuvenation. The collisional seismic models imply younger ages and higher masses than the seismic models based on single-star evolution.

AI.tldr: First asteroseismic modelling of SX Phoenicis blue stragglers in ω Centauri assuming a collisional merger origin, showing convective-core overshooting is key to rejuvenation and yielding younger, more massive models than single-star scenarios.
AI.motivation: Blue stragglers appear too massive and young for single-star evolution, and their formation channel is ambiguous. Asteroseismology offers the strongest constraints on internal structure, yet collisional-origin seismic modelling has been largely unexplored.
AI.method: Five SX Phe stars pulsating in two radial modes are studied. Parent-star evolution is computed with MESA; the collision is modelled with MMAMS, reconstructing the merger remnant via an entropic variable; post-merger evolution is evolved with MESA to the cluster age; seismic models are fitted to the two observed radial frequencies. A binary mass-transfer scenario is also tested for one star.
AI.result: Convective-core overshooting is essential but not always sufficient for rejuvenation. Rejuvenation depends complexly on parent masses, metallicity and collision time, giving three behaviours: no, delayed, and immediate rejuvenation. Collisional seismic models imply younger ages and higher masses than single-star-based models.
AI.conclusion: Collisional formation provides a viable, seismically testable channel for these blue stragglers, and the resulting models differ systematically (younger age, higher mass) from single-star interpretations, motivating wider use of asteroseismology to discriminate formation histories.

title: Symbolic Regression Fitting for Roche Lobe Radius
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables, Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: We present a compact approximation to the dimensionless, volume-equivalent Roche lobe radius $R_{\rm L}/a$, obtained by applying symbolic regression to radii calculated from the full Roche potential. Over $10^{-5}\leq q\leq10^5$, the expression reduces the root mean square error from $1.97\times10^{-3}$ for Eggleton's formula to $5.95\times10^{-4}$, while its maximum relative error is $1.39\%$, compared with Eggleton's $0.83\%$. Calculations at additional mass ratios give a mean relative error of $0.331\%$. The formula is monotonic, recovers the $q^{\frac{1}{3}}$ scaling at small mass ratio, and approaches a large-mass-ratio limit within $0.036\%$ of the limiting Roche model. In a NumPy float64 benchmark of $10^7$ direct formula evaluations, the SR expression takes $0.217$~s compared with $0.450$~s for Eggleton, a speed-up of $2.08$. These results quantify the accuracy and evaluation cost of a compact algebraic alternative for binary-system calculations.

AI.tldr: A symbolic-regression fit to the volume-equivalent Roche lobe radius reduces RMS error versus Eggleton's formula by ~3x over 10^-5 ≤ q ≤ 10^5 and evaluates ~2.08x faster.
AI.motivation: Eggleton's widely used analytic formula for the volume-equivalent Roche lobe radius carries non-negligible error; the authors seek a compact algebraic alternative with improved global accuracy and cheaper evaluation for binary-system calculations.
AI.method: Symbolic regression is applied to Roche lobe radii computed from the full Roche potential, yielding a closed-form approximation to R_L/a over mass ratios 10^-5 to 10^5; accuracy (RMS, mean and maximum relative error) and NumPy float64 timing against Eggleton's formula are benchmarked.
AI.result: RMS error drops from 1.97e-3 (Eggleton) to 5.95e-4; maximum relative error is 1.39% versus Eggleton's 0.83%; mean relative error at additional mass ratios is 0.331%. The formula is monotonic, reproduces the q^(1/3) small-q scaling, and lies within 0.036% of the large-mass-ratio limit. On 10^7 evaluations it runs in 0.217 s versus 0.450 s (2.08x speed-up).
AI.conclusion: The SR expression offers a compact, monotonic, physically consistent alternative to Eggleton's formula, trading a slightly higher worst-case relative error for substantially lower RMS error and ~2x faster evaluation.

title: 2D and 3D unified RHD atmospheres and wind models of early B-supergiants including approximate NLTE effects
summary: B supergiants are evolved massive stars with low surface gravities and lower effective temperatures, with substantial radiation-driven winds. Generally, they have been studied assuming 1D spherical symmetry. We present the first multi-D unified atmosphere and wind models for B supergiants, especially investigating the effects of approximate NLTE ionization and subsurface turbulence on the atmosphere and wind dynamics. We computed multi-D box-in-a-star RHD unified atmosphere and wind simulations of 2D/3D early B supergiant models using a hybrid opacity approach. We calculated line opacities from approximate NLTE populations, including line scattering. We calculated the flux-, energy-, and Planck-mean line opacities separately from our large line database using Sobolev escape probabilities, assuming two-level atoms. The models develop a highly turbulent atmosphere with time-averaged turbulent velocities of ~ 40 - 55 km/s at the photosphere in the 2D simulations, and ~ 25 km/s in 3D. In the cooler B1, B1.5 models, the wind acceleration is more gradual than in the hotter B0 model, leading to a significantly higher maximum wind speed in the B0 model. Further, the approximate NLTE formalism strongly alters the ionization stratification in the wind compared to LTE, modifying the line force. Mass-loss rates obtained in the models are of order 10^-6 - 3 x 10^-6 solar masses per year. Including turbulent pressure in hydrodynamically consistent NLTE CMF steady-state 1D simulations with comparable parameters can produce higher mass-loss rates and lower terminal wind velocities than in corresponding models without turbulent velocity, in overall qualitative agreement with our multi-D simulations. Our calculations suggest that in the lower surface-gravity B supergiants, in addition to modifying the photospheric density scale heights, turbulent pressure also influences global properties of the wind.

AI.tldr: First multi-D unified atmosphere-and-wind RHD models of B supergiants, showing that subsurface turbulence and approximate NLTE ionization strongly shape both photospheric structure and global wind properties (mass loss, terminal velocity).
AI.motivation: B supergiants are evolved massive stars with low surface gravity, low effective temperature, and substantial radiation-driven winds, yet they have almost exclusively been modeled in 1D spherical symmetry. The effects of multi-dimensional turbulence and NLTE ionization on their atmosphere/wind dynamics remain unexplored.
AI.method: 2D/3D box-in-a-star RHD unified atmosphere-and-wind simulations of early B supergiants using a hybrid opacity approach. Line opacities are computed from approximate NLTE populations (including line scattering); flux-, energy-, and Planck-mean opacities are derived separately from a large line database via Sobolev escape probabilities assuming two-level atoms. Turbulent pressure is also added to hydrodynamically consistent NLTE CMF steady-state 1D models for comparison.
AI.result: Models develop a highly turbulent atmosphere, with time-averaged turbulent velocities of ~40–55 km/s at the photosphere in 2D (~25 km/s in 3D). Cooler B1/B1.5 models show more gradual wind acceleration than the hotter B0 model, which reaches a significantly higher maximum wind speed. Approximate NLTE strongly alters the wind ionization stratification relative to LTE, modifying the line force. Mass-loss rates are ~1e-6 to 3e-6 Msun/yr. Adding turbulent pressure in 1D NLTE CMF models yields higher mass-loss rates and lower terminal velocities, qualitatively matching the multi-D results.
AI.conclusion: In lower-surface-gravity B supergiants, turbulent pressure not only modifies photospheric density scale heights but also influences global wind properties, supporting the importance of multi-D, NLTE, turbulent treatments over classical 1D spherical models.

title: JWST/NIRISS-SOSS Spectroscopic Variability and Auroral Modelling of Warm Ultracool Dwarf LSR J1835+3259
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 15 pages, 14 figures
summary: Auroral variability in ultracool dwarfs (UCDs) has been proposed as a key source of optical and infrared modulation, yet its physical origin remains poorly understood. We present JWST Near Infrared Imager and Slitless Spectrograph/Single Object Slitless Spectroscopy (NIRISS/SOSS) time-series spectroscopy of the M8.5 UCD LSR J1835+3259. These observations probe the object's wavelength-dependent rotational variability, providing insight into the atmospheric processes underlying its infrared behaviour. Additional GTC/MEGARA optical spectra reveal that its H$α$ emission has declined markedly since earlier epochs, suggesting a reduced activity state during the JWST observations. We detect no emission from H$_3^+$ or absorption by hydronium in the NIRISS spectra. We use principal component analysis to identify two distinct modes of spectral variability: one dominated by FeH modulation near 1 $μ$m and another contributing broadband variability across the H and K bands. We find that no model atmosphere grid provides a reasonable fit to the average NIRISS spectrum. However, a blended model comprising an M-dwarf photosphere and a cooler blackbody component provides an improved fit to the mean spectrum, the broadband spectral energy distribution and the NIRISS broadband variability. By adding perturbations to PICASO model grids, we demonstrate that a combination of atmospheric heating and non-equilibrium chemistry can successfully mimic a blend of unperturbed photosphere and a blackbody, and that the presence of these effects may explain the unusual spectrum and variability of LSR J1835+3259.

AI.tldr: JWST NIRISS/SOSS time-series spectroscopy of the M8.5 ultracool dwarf LSR J1835+3259 reveals two modes of rotational variability and is best explained by a blend of an M-dwarf photosphere with a cooler blackbody component, which atmospheric heating plus non-equilibrium chemistry can reproduce.
AI.motivation: Auroral variability in ultracool dwarfs is proposed as a key driver of optical and infrared modulation, but its physical origin is poorly understood. The authors aim to characterize the wavelength-dependent rotational variability of LSR J1835+3259 and identify the atmospheric processes behind its infrared behavior.
AI.method: JWST NIRISS/SOSS time-series spectroscopy probes wavelength-dependent rotational variability; GTC/MEGARA optical spectra track H-alpha emission over epochs. Principal component analysis (PCA) decomposes spectral variability modes. Model fitting compares standard atmosphere grids with a blended M-dwarf photosphere + cooler blackbody model, and PICASO model grids are perturbed to test heating and non-equilibrium chemistry effects.
AI.result: H-alpha emission has declined markedly since earlier epochs, indicating a reduced activity state. No H3+ emission or hydronium absorption is detected. PCA identifies two variability modes: one dominated by FeH modulation near 1 micron and one broadband across H and K bands. No standard model atmosphere grid fits the mean NIRISS spectrum well; a blended M-dwarf photosphere + cooler blackbody improves fits to the mean spectrum, the broadband SED, and the NIRISS broadband variability. Perturbed PICASO grids show atmospheric heating plus non-equilibrium chemistry can mimic such a blend.
AI.conclusion: The unusual spectrum and variability of LSR J1835+3259 are consistent with a combination of atmospheric heating and non-equilibrium chemistry producing an effective photosphere-blackbody blend, offering a plausible physical explanation for its auroral-related infrared modulation.

title: Properties of near-surface turbulence in hot, massive stars: Statistical signatures from multi-dimensional models of O-type stars
summary: Variability of massive stars indicates the presence of complex, multi-D physics near the surface. Recent advancements in multi-D radiation-hydrodynamical modelling of massive star atmospheres show strong turbulence triggered by the iron opacity bump. We analyze statistical properties of sub-surface turbulence in multi-D simulations of O-star atmospheres. Particularly, we study potential dependencies of turbulent properties on global stellar parameters. Using 2D O-star models, we studied several statistical properties of the turbulence that develops in these models. We compute autocorrelation functions of density and velocity to study typical eddy length scales. Moreover, we compute kinetic energy power spectra to analyze the energy distribution and compare this to known results from established turbulence theories. We find anisotropy of the turbulent eddies in velocity space. Moreover, this anisotropy increases with classical Eddington factor. This anisotropy disappears in density space where all models show nearly isotropic structures and no dependence on stellar parameters. The kinetic energy power spectra exhibit an inertial range with a cascade exponent that has an average value of -2.57. This exponent does not show any clear dependence on stellar parameters. Importantly, this energy cascade is significantly steeper than those in known turbulence theories such as Kolmogorov turbulence with exponent -5/3 and Burgers turbulence with exponent -2. This additional steepening can potentially be attributed to radiative damping which increases with increasing wavenumber. Sub-surface turbulence in hot, massive stars is anisotropic and radially dominated in velocity space and its energy cascade is steeper than both Kolmogorov turbulence and Burgers turbulence. Although not rigorously proven here, we suggest that this steepening is due to the scale-dependent effect of radiative damping.

AI.tldr: Statistical analysis of sub-surface turbulence in 2D radiation-hydrodynamical O-star atmosphere models reveals radially dominated anisotropic velocity eddies (increasing with Eddington factor) and an inertial-range kinetic energy cascade with exponent ≈ -2.57, steeper than Kolmogorov (-5/3) or Burgers (-2), likely due to scale-dependent radiative damping.
AI.motivation: Multi-D modelling shows massive-star atmospheres host strong turbulence driven by the iron opacity bump, but the statistical nature of this sub-surface turbulence and its dependence on global stellar parameters remain unclear.
AI.method: Using 2D O-star models, the authors compute autocorrelation functions of density and velocity to infer typical eddy length scales, and kinetic energy power spectra to characterize energy distribution, comparing results against established turbulence theories.
AI.result: Velocity-space eddies are anisotropic, with anisotropy increasing with the classical Eddington factor; density-space structures are nearly isotropic and parameter-independent. Kinetic energy spectra show an inertial range with mean cascade exponent -2.57, with no clear dependence on stellar parameters—significantly steeper than Kolmogorov (-5/3) and Burgers (-2).
AI.conclusion: Sub-surface turbulence in hot massive stars is anisotropic and radially dominated in velocity space, with a steeper energy cascade than standard turbulence theories; the steepening is plausibly attributed to scale-dependent radiative damping, though not rigorously proven.

title: Zeeman-Doppler imaging of V889 Her: Surface spots and magnetic field topology 2017 - 2023
summary: The surface magnetic field of the young solar analogue V889 Her is studied using Zeeman-Doppler imaging (ZDI). This well-studied star has previously been reported to have an exceptionally high differential rotation and show abrupt changes in the surface magnetic field and spot configuration. Our aim is to study the evolution of the magnetic field topology in V889 Her. This will contribute to understanding dynamo action in young solar-type stars. We also want to constrain the surface differential rotation curve of the target star.Methods. We employ the ZDI method on observations collected with the SOFIN spectropolarimeter mounted at the Nordic Optical Telescope. We test differential rotation parameters previously reported in studies of the star. We observe significant changes in the radial field near the rotational pole throughout the whole span of the observations. Specifically, the polarity of the radial field is reversed around 2021. The large-scale magnetic field also contains a persistent strong azimuthal component at high latitudes. We detect abrupt changes in the spot configuration in June 2018 on the time scale of a week. The observations favour a solar type differential rotation. The different rotation parameters influence the brightness map more than the magnetic field topology. We cannot link the observed changes in the magnetic field topology with the evolution of the long-term spot activity. The abrupt changes observed in 2018 confirm previous reports that the surface magnetic field and spot configuration may undergo rapid evolution on short time scales. This complicates the estimation of the surface differential rotation.

AI.tldr: Using Zeeman-Doppler imaging on the young solar analogue V889 Her, the study tracks the evolution of its large-scale surface magnetic field topology, reporting a polarity reversal of the polar radial field near 2021, a persistent high-latitude azimuthal component, and abrupt week-scale spot changes in 2018, while the data favor a solar-type differential rotation.
AI.motivation: V889 Her is a well-studied young solar analogue previously reported to show exceptionally high differential rotation and abrupt changes in its surface magnetic field and spot configuration. Understanding how its magnetic topology evolves helps constrain dynamo action in young solar-type stars and clarifies the surface differential rotation curve.
AI.method: Zeeman-Doppler imaging (ZDI) applied to spectropolarimetric observations taken with the SOFIN spectropolarimeter at the Nordic Optical Telescope. Previously reported differential rotation parameters are tested against the data.
AI.result: Significant changes in the radial field near the rotational pole are observed across the whole observation span, including a polarity reversal around 2021. The large-scale field has a persistent strong azimuthal component at high latitudes. Abrupt spot-configuration changes occur in June 2018 on a week-long timescale. Observations favor a solar-type differential rotation; rotation parameters affect the brightness map more than the magnetic topology. No link is found between the magnetic topology changes and long-term spot activity evolution.
AI.conclusion: The rapid field and spot evolution in 2018 confirms earlier reports of short-timescale surface changes, which complicates the estimation of surface differential rotation. Magnetic topology changes cannot be tied to long-term spot activity evolution.

title: Density fluctuations in pseudo-streamer and helmet streamer: Generation, propagation and comparison with Metis observations
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures; Accepted for publication in MNRAS on 12 November, 2026
summary: Recent white-light observations from the Metis coronagraph on board Solar Orbiter have shown the presence of propagating density fluctuations with a period of $\sim5$ minutes, particularly in the observationally bright regions of helmet streamers and pseudo-streamers. These density fluctuations have been shown to originate from magnetohydrodynamic wave modes -- slow and fast modes can directly compress the plasma, whereas Alfvén waves generate density fluctuations via a non-linear coupling with the slow and fast modes. In general, in low plasma $β$ regions, slow modes contribute more towards the generation of density fluctuations, whereas in high $β$ regions, there are significant contributions from both slow and fast waves. In this work, we investigate the propagation of (non-linear) Alfvén waves and the associated density fluctuations using a 2.5D axisymmetric global solar wind model that includes two distinct magnetic field topologies -- a helmet streamer and a pseudo-streamer. Key differences in these magnetic configurations give rise to differences in the wave behaviour due to, for example, the presence of a current sheet in the helmet streamer and an X-type null point in the pseudo-streamer, and the structure of the $β= 1$ layer in both magnetic field configurations. This leads to the possible creation of prominent interference patterns along the helmet streamer axis, which do not appear along the pseudo-streamer axis. Unlike in the streamer region, we also find that along the pseudo-streamer axis, the contribution to the density fluctuations is due to the fast waves only, despite being in a low $β$ plasma.

AI.tldr: A 2.5D axisymmetric global solar wind model compares how non-linear Alfvén waves generate density fluctuations in a helmet streamer versus a pseudo-streamer, finding topology-dependent wave behaviour including interference patterns along the helmet streamer axis and fast-wave-dominated density fluctuations along the pseudo-streamer axis despite low plasma β.
AI.motivation: Metis coronagraph observations on Solar Orbiter reveal ~5-minute propagating density fluctuations in bright helmet-streamer and pseudo-streamer regions. These fluctuations arise from MHD wave modes (compressible slow/fast modes, or Alfvén waves via non-linear coupling). Since the magnetic topologies of helmet streamers (current sheet) and pseudo-streamers (X-type null point) differ, the authors aim to understand how these distinct configurations affect non-linear Alfvén wave propagation and the resulting density fluctuations.
AI.method: A 2.5D axisymmetric global solar wind model is used, incorporating two distinct magnetic field topologies: a helmet streamer and a pseudo-streamer. The model investigates the propagation of non-linear Alfvén waves and the associated density fluctuations, examining key differences arising from the current sheet in the helmet streamer, the X-type null point in the pseudo-streamer, and the structure of the β = 1 layer in each configuration.
AI.result: Differences in magnetic configuration produce differences in wave behaviour. Prominent interference patterns form along the helmet streamer axis but do not appear along the pseudo-streamer axis. Along the pseudo-streamer axis, density fluctuations are attributed to fast waves only, despite the low β plasma—unlike in the streamer region where slow modes generally dominate in low β.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic topology (current sheet vs. X-type null point, and the β = 1 layer structure) critically governs the propagation of non-linear Alfvén waves and the generation of density fluctuations. The pseudo-streamer's fast-wave-only contribution in low β contrasts with standard expectations and with helmet-streamer behaviour, highlighting the importance of global magnetic configuration in interpreting coronagraphic density-fluctuation observations.

title: A New Galactic Close Binary Supersoft Source Candidate
comment: Accepted for publication on MNRAS as a Letter
summary: The identification of a new galactic Close Binary Supersoft Source (CBSS) candidate, whose main ID is ZTF J043609.49+364057.7, is presented on the basis of the analysis of its optical spectrum, light curve and Spectral Energy Distribution (SED). During a survey designed to find candidates to the aforementioned class independently of X-ray emissions, this object's optical spectrum was found to exhibit the typical emission features expected for a CBSS. The available photometric data show a quasi-sinusoidal modulation, with a period of 5.42 h, compatible with the orbital modulation of the system. Although there is no current identification of X-ray emission from this source, its SED displays a highly absorbed bright FUV component, given the estimated E(B - V) ~ 0.7 mag.

AI.tldr: A new Galactic Close Binary Supersoft Source candidate, ZTF J043609.49+364057.7, is identified from optical spectroscopy, a 5.42 h quasi-sinusoidal modulation, and a highly absorbed FUV-dominated SED.
AI.motivation: CBSSs are traditionally found via X-ray surveys; the authors aim to find them independently of X-ray emission, since a CBSS may be X-ray quiet or heavily absorbed.
AI.method: Analysis of the optical spectrum (searched for typical CBSS emission features), photometric light curve (period search / modulation), and the Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) with reddening estimate E(B−V) ~ 0.7 mag.
AI.result: Optical spectrum shows the characteristic emission features of a CBSS; photometry reveals a quasi-sinusoidal modulation with P = 5.42 h, consistent with orbital modulation; no current X-ray identification, but the SED exhibits a highly absorbed, bright FUV component.
AI.conclusion: ZTF J043609.49+364057.7 is a strong CBSS candidate, demonstrating that an X-ray-independent, optically-driven selection can uncover such systems; follow-up X-ray observations are warranted.
